procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.04.2022 in CRLOP Nos.3470 and 5767 of 2019
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court rejected the prayer for quashing of criminal complaints qua the appellant in connection with the offence punishable u/s. 138 r/w. s.142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Aggrieved by the rejection of the petition for quashing of criminal complaints, the appellant filed an appeal in the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeal Nos. 1577-1578 of 2024). The Supreme Court issued notice and granted a stay of further proceedings qua the appellant on 12th December 2022. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the appeals.

directions: The judgment and order passed by the High Court dated 26th April, 2022 is quashed and set aside.

The proceedings in CC Nos. 3151 and 3150 of 2017 on the file of learned XVIII Metropolitan Magistrate, Saidapet, Chennai (now transferred to the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Fast Track Court-III, Saidapet, Chennai) in connection with the offence punishable under Section 138 read with Section 142 of the N.I. Act are quashed and set aside qua the present appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the criminal proceedings initiated against the appellant for an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, should be quashed.

facts: A company issued five cheques to a complainant, which were subsequently dishonored with the reason 'payment stopped by drawer'.
The complainant filed criminal complaints under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (N.I. Act) against the company, the signatory of the cheques, and the appellant (a director).
The appellant was not the signatory to the cheques in question.
The appellant's request to quash the criminal proceedings against her was rejected by the High Court, leading to the present appeal before the Supreme Court.
law: The key legal provision is Section 141 of the N.I. Act, which establishes the principle of vicarious liability for directors of a company.

For a director to be held vicariously liable for an offence committed by the company under Section 138, the complaint must contain specific allegations (averments) that the director was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the company's business at the time the offence was committed.
Merely being a director is not sufficient to make a person liable under this provision.
application: The Supreme Court examined the contents of the criminal complaints filed by the respondent.
It found that the complaints lacked the specific averments required to invoke Section 141 of the N.I. Act against the appellant.

The Court noted that it was not the complainant's case that the appellant was the Managing Director or Joint Managing Director, nor was there any allegation that she was involved in the day-to-day affairs of the company.

The Court accepted the appellant's argument that she was not a signatory to the cheques and that the allegations in the complaint were insufficient to hold her vicariously liable for the company's actions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the averments in the criminal complaints were insufficient to establish the appellant's vicarious liability under Section 141 of the N.I. Act. Therefore, the Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and quashed the criminal proceedings against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the criminal proceedings initiated against the appellant for an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, should be quashed.
appellant_arguments: The appellant is an aged lady and was not involved in the day-to-day affairs of the Company.
The complaint does not contain any averments that the appellant was in charge of the day-to-day affairs of the Company.
The appellant was not a signatory to the cheque in question; only accused No. 2 was the signatory.
Consequently, the High Court erred in not quashing the criminal complaints against the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The High Court correctly dismissed the petition to quash the criminal complaints after considering the material on record.
The grounds raised by the appellant are a matter of defense and can only be raised at the trial stage.
Therefore, no interference by the Supreme Court is warranted in the appeal.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana v. Brij Lal Mittal and others
cases.principle: For making a Director of a Company liable for offences committed by the Company under Section 141 of the NI Act, there must be specific averments against the Director showing how and in what manner the Director was responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. Merely reproducing the words of the section is insufficient.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Merely reproducing the words of a statute is insufficient to make a director vicariously liable for a company's offence; the complaint must contain a clear statement of fact as to how and in what manner the director was responsible for the conduct of the company's business.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The criminal proceedings against the appellant must be quashed because the complaint fails to make the necessary averments for vicarious liability. The complaint contains only a bald statement that the appellant was a director, but explicitly states that another accused (Accused No. 2) was the authorized signatory who was in-charge of and responsible for the day-to-day affairs of the company. In the absence of any specific allegation that the appellant was also in charge of and responsible for the company's business, no prima facie case is made out against her.
legal_tests_applied: For a director of a company to be held liable for offences under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the complaint must contain a specific allegation that the director was in charge of the company and also responsible to the company for the conduct of its business.

A bald statement in the complaint that a person was a director of the company is not sufficient to make them liable; there must be a clear and specific averment indicating their role in the company's business.
